- Three top-level groups in this order: <g id="far">, <g id="mid">, <g id="near">. Inside them, one named group per
  object (lowercase snake_case: table, chair_3, wall_screen, window_2). Draw the walls and the floor complete behind
  the furniture, so nothing has a hole when the layers slide apart.
- Light and surface effects go in classed groups inside each depth group: class="lm-shadow" (cast and contact
  shadows), class="lm-light" (light patches), class="lm-atmos" (haze, light shafts), class="lm-texture" (texture

THE WORLD: CORPORATE OFFICE
The fourth floor of a converted 1920s brick textile mill in a temperate city, now the head office of a 180-person insurance and operations company. One long open floor about 60 m by 18 m inside, about 4.2 m from floor to the underside of the joists (an old spinning floor, much taller than a modern office), with rooms built inside it as glass and birch-ply boxes.
Architecture:
- white-painted brick walls with the courses still visible; one end wall left as bare red-brown brick
- a regular grid of black steel columns, two rows, about 6.7 m apart along the floor and 4.7 m across the bays, with riveted caps; dark timber beams and joists overhead
- exposed services hung below the joists, never a suspended ceiling: sprinkler pipes painted dark red with small sprinkler heads, cable trays, round ducts, linear pendant lights
- tall steel-sash factory windows in a long regular row on the south wall: each about 1.8 m wide and 2.1 m high, 20 small panes (5 across, 4 high) in thin dark-green-painted steel bars, one centre-pivoting hopper pane per window, a deep concrete sill at about 0.9 m
- the original floor: wide sanded maple boards, patched where machines once stood, with flat-weave rugs marking zones
- rooms built inside the floor are boxes of birch-ply frame and glass that rise to the joists on a slim steel head track (the joists, the sprinkler pipe and the cable trays run on above them); glass walls run past the columns without touching them; every glass wall carries two frosted manifestation bands, at about 0.9 m and 1.5 m above the floor (plain bands, no words or logos)
Materials: birch ply and oak furniture, black powder-coated steel, white and bare brick, sanded maple boards, felt and wool upholstery in slate blue and oat, brass lamp fittings, deep green as the company's colour (a painted wall, felt panels), with signal red only on the few things that are red in life (the sprinkler pipe, a fire extinguisher)
Scale (draw to these real sizes; a person is about 1.75 m):
- a person is about 1.75 m tall: the ceiling joists are at 2.4 times a person's height; a door is 2.1 m high and about 0.9 m wide
- desk tops at 0.73 m, kitchen worktops at 0.9 m, a standing reception counter at about 1.05 m, a seat at 0.45 m
- desks are 1.6 m by 0.8 m per person; four make a back-to-back cluster of 3.2 m by 1.6 m; main walkways about 1.5 m wide
- a wall screen in a meeting room is a 65 to 75 inch screen (about 1.5 m wide) with its centre about 1.3 m above the floor
- a fire extinguisher hangs on a bracket with its handle about 1 m above the floor; green exit signs with a running figure and an arrow (no words) sit above exit doors, 2.2 to 2.4 m up, above the door head
Signs of life (every set shows someone works here):
- work in progress everywhere: printed charts pinned up (empty slots, no text), sticky notes in clusters, archive boxes, labelled trays (no letters)
- personal things: a cardigan on a chair back, mismatched mugs, a framed photo turned to face the desk, a small cactus
- infrastructure of a real office: cable trays and floor boxes, monitor arms, a first-aid box, a fire extinguisher by a column, coat hooks, an umbrella stand
- slight wear: scuffs on the floor along the walking line, a rug corner turned up, a chair with a lower back than the others
Default light: Mid-afternoon in late autumn: low sun from the south windows throws long patches of warm light, broken by the 20-pane grid, across the floor and furniture; daylight away from the windows reads slightly cool and blue; the deep side of the floor is lit by warm linear pendants.
Outside: The view through the windows: low brick terraces, slate roofs, one chimney stack, a few bare trees, a pale sky; no landmarks, no signs.
Motifs: Use at least three of these in every scene so the sets belong to one place (each scene names the ones its camera can see): the 20-pane steel window and its light pattern, a black steel column, white and bare brick, birch-ply joinery, the exposed dark red sprinkler pipe and cable tray, one deep green element, one brass lamp or fitting.

OBJECTS: every object must be a real, recognisable thing built the way the real one is built. A chair is

- desk: 1.6 by 0.8 m top at 0.73 m on a steel frame, a cable tray under the back edge, a monitor arm clamped to the back edge

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- an attempt at photorealism
- busy detail behind where the head will be
- plastic gradients on everything
- uncanny over-rendering
Not in this world:
- a generic glass-tower office with no character
- real brands, logos, signs with words, flags or anything that pins a country
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- a catalogue-clean room: every scene shows someone works here
- windows with a few huge panes or modern casements
- screens that face a window or sit with a window right behind them (glare): screens sit at about 90 degrees to the windows
- columns at uneven spacing, or columns standing inside a glass wall
- a low or tiled ceiling anywhere: the floor is 4.2 m high with exposed services, and the rooms built inside it rise to the joists
